other_side: Zitron's summer reads the opposite way. Where NLW sees agents 'killing the bubble math' and markets rightly rewarding Microsoft and Nvidia, Zitron pulls together analyst notes from Wells Fargo, Barclays and UBS estimating that seventy per cent or more of the hyperscalers' AI revenue comes from just two customers, OpenAI and Anthropic, both loss-making and both dependent on raising roughly a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single year to pay their compute bills. He argues that outside those two there is no demand remotely close to the capacity being built, that the record one-day gains are capital being extracted from the system rather than evidence of end-customer return, and that there are 'few signs that these companies can be sold to anyone or taken public' — a direct challenge to the two-trillion-dollar IPO NLW calls the prelude to the autumn.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether end customers, not investors, are paying for the compute. Both accept as fact that OpenAI and Anthropic are unprofitable, that they account for the bulk of hyperscaler AI growth, and that per-seat pricing never justified the capex. The empirical question that will resolve is whether enterprise spend on agents becomes a large, diversified, self-funding line item; the observable is a hyperscaler breaking out AI revenue by customer, or an S-1 from Anthropic showing gross margin after compute. The worldview residue is whether concentrated, subsidised demand is a bridge or a cliff. NLW is vindicated if the IPO prices near two trillion on disclosed, non-circular revenue and holds. Zitron is vindicated if the IPO slips, or prices on revenue that turns out to be hyperscaler money round-tripped. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: the customer base is dangerously narrow and nobody is disclosing it.
